body.heading: Why stand-ins?
paragraphs: Imagine if we could never use stand-in words: 'Maya picked up Maya's book and Maya gave the book to Ben, and Ben thanked Maya.' Exhausting! Pronouns step in so sentences can breathe: 'Maya picked up her book and gave it to Ben, and he thanked her.'
Here are the seven hardest-working stand-ins in English.

body.heading: Talking about myself and you
paragraphs: I — I am seven. Use I when you talk about yourself.
You — You are my friend. Use you when you talk to someone.
We — We play together. Use we when you mean yourself and others.

body.heading: Talking about others
paragraphs: He — He is my brother. Use he for a boy or a man.
She — She is my teacher. Use she for a girl or a woman.
It — It is a puppy. Use it for an animal or a thing.
They — They are my cousins. Use they for two or more people, animals or things.

body.heading: Think and talk
paragraphs: 1. Tell a three-sentence story about your best friend without using their name — only he or she. Can your listener guess who it is?
2. Point to things and people around you and label each one: I, you, he, she, it or they.

takeaway: Pronouns — I, you, he, she, it, we, they — stand in for names so sentences stay smooth.
